extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy of science, naturalists, taxonomists, and scientific investigators interested in terminology and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for creating precise descriptive terminology, systematic nomenclature, and natural classifications that best serve induction and the growth of scientific knowledge. Covers when to prefer mechanical/technical language versus richly meaningful terms, and how to choose classifying properties and diagnostic marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact and extensive descriptive terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive language should be exact and extensive enough to place on record individual observations with precision (e.g., botany: every part named; mineralogy: lustre, hardness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: botanical terminology distinguishing calyx, corolla, stamens, pistils and many leaf shapes (pinnatifid, pinnatipartite, etc.); Werner's classified scale of colors; Mohs' numerical hardness scale. Use definitions, combinations, and numerical relations where appropriate to convey precise form and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin concise names for recurring abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparison of phenomena leads to a new common conception, give it a concise name to promote perspicuity and fix attention (e.g., 'circle', 'limit', 'momentum').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise terms save intellectual effort and memory, allowing the mind to focus on relations among concepts instead of re-stating complex definitions; useful whenever a conceived abstraction will be often spoken of or leads to many consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a name for every Kind (systematic nomenclature)
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be a name for every Kind (lowest kinds/inferma species) with which a branch of knowledge is conversant; nomenclature should be systematic where species are numerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science examples: Linnæan nomenclature for plants and animals; chemical nomenclature from French chemists. When new lowest kinds are discovered, assign names consistently according to the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature terms must connote both Kind and distinguishing attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in a nomenclature connote not only certain attributes but also that those attributes are distinctive of a Kind; definitions should enumerate characters sufficient to distinguish the Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition together with the form of the name (indicating infima species) unfolds meaning; names may be revised if the set of distinguishing characters proves inadequate or non-unique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology should promote perspicuity and fixed senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology should fix the sense of terms so the same word is used in the same sense and the same idea is always expressed by the same words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Tournefort and Linnæus fixed botanical language to shed 'clearness and precision' over the science. Avoid ambiguous re-use of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mechanical/technical language when subject permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the nature of the subject permits reasoning to be carried on mechanically, the language should be constructed on as mechanical principles as possible (e.g., algebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical symbolical language is ideal for subjects reducible to relations of numbers because it enables purely mechanical manipulation of symbols and compact representation of operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical/empty signs in non-mechanical subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: In subjects where mechanical use of language would be dangerous, construct language so as to make mechanical use difficult and to keep meaning constantly in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-mathematical sciences require concrete mental images of phenomena during induction and much of deduction; over-abstraction into meaningless counters risks losing touch with particulars and leads to misapplication of formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed meaning in word formation via derivation and analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: As much meaning as possible should be thrown into the formation of the word itself using derivation and analogy, preferably from native roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Languages forming compounds from native roots (e.g., German, Greek) better preserve relations between primitive and derivative meanings, helping users retain a consciousness of what terms signify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative measures where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When properties admit of numerical measurement, supply numerical scales to render comparisons exact (e.g., Mohs hardness, specific gravity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical measures give immediate and comparable information; when possible, define properties so they provide numerical values or require mathematical calculation for precise relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep terminology alive by continual acquaintance with phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid living only among formulæ; continually revive the meaning of terms by habitual contemplation of the phenomena themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on formulas causes their practical meaning to fade and leads to misapplication; maintain direct study of cases so that terms remain linked to their referents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should order ideas to aid induction and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is a contrivance for arranging objects into groups and ordering those groups so as to best conduce to remembrance and the ascertainment of their laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is to cause ideas to accompany or succeed one another to give greatest command over acquired knowledge and lead most directly to the acquisition of more; naming is secondary to this arranging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer classifications that enable many and important general propositions (natural classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific (natural) classifications should group objects so that a greater number of general and important propositions can be made about them than by other possible groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural classifications correspond to the general aspect and spontaneous tendencies of the mind; they should place together objects most similar in their overall properties rather than by an arbitrary single property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose classifying properties that are causes or sure marks of many other properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, base classification on properties that are causes of many other properties, or at least sure marks of them, because such properties better indicate other shared attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes are preferable as they are the surest and most direct marks; if the cause is not directly diagnostic, select prominent effects of the cause to serve as marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial classifications founded on trivial or arbitrary properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not persist with classifications founded on simple, easily perceived, but unimportant properties which do not lead to useful generalizations (e.g., classifying plants solely by number of stamens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such technical/artificial classifications may be convenient for certain identifications but can be 'mischievous' if they habitually direct thought away from groups with more significant shared properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must consider the whole range of real objects
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute classes properly, one must take into consideration all really existing objects with any affinity to the item being classified; classifications relate to real, not merely imaginable, objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No family or general arrangement can be rationally constituted without reference to the placement of those groups within the general division of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide systematic and uniform naming for newly discovered taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: When new lowest Kinds are discovered, names should be given on a uniform principle so the nomenclature remains systematic and usable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the utility of the nomenclature and allows the continued making of predicates about the Kind; examples include botanical and chemical naming systems.
